newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-OECD offers Moscow new ties, not membership.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-OECD offers Moscow new ties, not membership.

text.p: The OECD, offering Moscow a closer partnership but no firm date for joining the international free-market organisation, signed a new cooperation pact with Russia on Tuesday and vowed to help it liberalise its economy.
Canadian OECD Secretary General Donald Johnston signed the deal with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov calling for new liaison ties to encourage a transition away from Soviet-era planning.

An OECD statement released after a brief signing ceremony pledged to "assist the Russian Federation in its progress to establishing a fully fledged market economy within a framework of democratic institutions".

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development also promised to "help the Russian Federation to meet and sustain all the conditions for membership of the OECD," without giving a target date for Russia to join.
The deal, signed under the shadow of a NATO-Russia summit a few miles way, takes Moscow a step closer to joining the body set up 50 years ago to help western Europe to its feet after World War II.
But while the OECD has accepted the principle of welcoming Russia in, diplomats said membership looks some way off as Moscow slowly adapts to the group's free-market ideology.
"There is no way Russia is going to meet OECD standards for joining in any swift way," a senior OECD source said.
"This signifies that we recognise their importance but without opening formal negotiations at all," he added.
Russia surprised the OECD with a formal membership bid at the group's last ministerial meeting a year ago.
Membership could help its finances by improving its standing with banks and creditors, and give it direct access to Western economic policy discussions through powerful OECD committees.
The OECD has embraced former Soviet bloc states such as Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland and is negotiating with Slovakia.

An OECD communique issued on Tuesday at the end of its two-day annual summit said Russian membership was the ultimate "shared goal". But Johnston had said ahead of the meeting Moscow had a long way to go on economic liberalisation before formal entry talks could start.

The OECD has had some form of cooperation with Russia since 1990, as part of its mandate to help economies in transition. The two sides also signed a declaration on cooperation on June 8, 1994, opening up some policy dialogue.
The new framework calls for two high-level meetings yearly, one of those at ministerial level, Johnston said last week.
Primakov was in Paris with President Boris Yeltsin who met U.S. President Bill Clinton to sign a landmark security pact between Russia and NATO.

The OECD's membership profile has changed dramatically in the past few years as it opened its doors to three eastern European countries as well as Mexico, and also spread its wings in Asia beyond Japan to include most recently South Korea, swelling its ranks to 29 nations.
